Several outcomes would then have distinct interpretations. A small number of narrow, agecoherent metallicity groups with bulge-like chemistry and no globular-cluster light-element anomalies would favour a substantial BFF-like component. Multiple such groups with differing kinematics could instead point toward assembly from several massive inner-Galaxy fragments. An old population rich in Na–O or related globular-cluster anomalies would favour a larger contribution from inspiralling genuine globular clusters. Finally, a chemically continuous distribution following the bulge sequence, combined with age and kinematic gradients rather than discrete groups, would favour repeated in-situ star formation plus migration from the surrounding inner Galaxy. 

The α-element test is already capable of ruling out the simplest version of the hypothesis. If the supersolar NSC population were directly analogous to the younger metal-rich component in Terzan 5, approximately solar [α/Fe] would be expected. The existence of supersolar-metallicity, Si-enhanced NSC stars (Thorsbro et al. 2020) therefore demands either a different enrichment timescale, additional gas infall, or a mixture of populations. The NSC may still contain an early BFF-like component, but the present-day cluster is unlikely to be a straightforward surviving copy of Terzan 5 or Liller 1.

## **R. Michael Rich**[1] **, Brian Thorsbro**[2] _[,]_[3] **, and Christian I. Johnson**[4] 

1Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of California, Los Angeles, CA 90095-1547, USA 

2Division of Astrophysics, Department of Physics, Lund University, Box 118, SE-22100 Lund, Sweden 

3Universit´e Cˆote d’Azur, Observatoire de la Cˆote d’Azur, CNRS, Laboratoire Lagrange, 06000 Nice, France 

4Space Telescope Science Institute, 3700 San Martin Drive, Baltimore, MD 21218, USA 

**Abstract.** The Milky Way nuclear star cluster (NSC) is unlike a conventional globular cluster: it contains a broad metallicity distribution and stellar populations formed over an extended interval, while its detailed abundances show a close connection to the inner Galactic bulge. We ask whether the NSC should instead be compared with the proposed “bulge fossil fragments” Terzan 5 and Liller 1, complex stellar systems interpreted as surviving remnants of massive structures involved in early bulge assembly. We place this comparison against the field-bulge metallicity distribution measured by the Blanco DECam Bulge Survey and against high-resolution infrared abundance measurements in the NSC. A broad metallicity distribution by itself is not diagnostic, because the bulge field is intrinsically broad and strongly structured. More discriminating tests are the presence of chemically narrow and age-coherent subpopulations, the relation between [α/Fe] and [Fe/H], light-element abundance patterns, spatial segregation, and chemo-dynamical differences among populations. Existing NSC data establish strong chemical links with the bulge but do not support a simple one-to-one analogue of either Terzan 5 or Liller 1. In particular, metal-rich α-enhanced stars in the NSC provide an important contrast with the near-solar [α/Fe] metal-rich populations of the best-studied fossil-fragment candidates. We argue that the BFF hypothesis is most useful as a falsifiable framework for identifying an early bulge-building component within a composite NSC assembled through in-situ star formation, migration, and cluster infall. 

**Keywords.** Galaxy: bulge, Galaxy: center, Galaxy: nucleus, stars: abundances, globular clusters: general

## **6. Summary and outlook** 

The comparison among the field bulge, bulge fossil fragments, and the NSC provides a useful way to organise the rapidly expanding Galactic-centre abundance data. The BDBS fieldbulge sample shows that a broad or even structured metallicity distribution is not by itself evidence for discrete fossil populations (Johnson et al. 2022). Terzan 5 and Liller 1 demonstrate what stronger evidence looks like: chemically and chronologically distinct populations, bulgelike enrichment patterns, and an absence of the light-element anticorrelations that characterise genuine globular clusters (Origlia et al. 2011; Ferraro et al. 2021; Alvarez Garay et al. 2024; Zullo et al. 2026). 

The NSC shares important properties with both comparison classes. Its broad metallicity distribution and detailed abundances link it strongly to the inner bulge (Rich et al. 2017; Ryde et al. 2025), while its extended star-formation history and chemical heterogeneity resemble the complexity that motivated the BFF interpretation of Terzan 5 and Liller 1. At the same time, the metal-rich α-enhanced population found by Thorsbro et al. (2020) shows that the analogy cannot be exact. 

The decisive next step is therefore not simply more metallicities, but multi-dimensional chemical tagging. High-resolution infrared spectra should identify candidate NSC components in [Fe/H], α elements, and light elements, followed by age, spatial, and kinematic tests of those same groups. The ELT may eventually test for multiple old main-sequence turnoffs in the NSC, analogous to those resolved in Terzan 5 and Liller 1. In this form the BFF hypothesis is falsifiable: it predicts coherent stellar populations rather than merely a broad MDF. Whether or not the NSC ultimately qualifies as a bulge fossil fragment, these tests will quantify how much of the nucleus was inherited from early bulge building blocks, how much arrived through cluster infall, and how much formed in situ at the Galactic centre.

## **2. What does a bulge fossil fragment look like?** 

Terzan 5 provides the clearest chemical benchmark. High-resolution spectroscopy established distinct iron-abundance populations and different α-element behaviour: the subsolar component is α-enhanced, while the metal-rich component has approximately solar [α/Fe], consistent with enrichment on a longer timescale that included Type Ia supernovae (Origlia et al. 2011). Its metallicity distribution is demonstrably multi-modal rather than that of a monometallic globular cluster (Massari et al. 2014). Photometry subsequently showed distinct main-sequence turnoffs, with the principal subsolar population being old and the supersolar population several Gyr younger (Ferraro et al. 2016). New JWST photometry now resolves the turnoff region particularly clearly, giving ages of 12 _._ 5 _±_ 0 _._ 5 Gyr and 4 _._ 7 _±_ 0 _._ 5 Gyr for the two principal components, with evidence for still younger stars (Zullo et al. 2026). 

Liller 1 exhibits the same qualitative combination of an old population and a much younger component. Deep photometry identifies an old population near 12 Gyr and a young component formed only a few Gyr ago, motivating its inclusion with Terzan 5 in the BFF class (Ferraro et al. 2021). Recent high-resolution spectroscopy strengthens the analogy: Liller 1 contains chemically distinct subsolar and supersolar populations, but its old component does not show the Na–O anticorrelation characteristic of genuine globular clusters (Alvarez Garay et al. 2024). Terzan 5 likewise lacks the light-element anticorrelation expected for an ordinary globular cluster in the existing high-resolution samples (Origlia et al. 2011).

Among Type II GCs, M22 (NGC 6656) is one of the most extensively studied examples. Spectroscopic investigations have firmly established the presence of internal variations in iron, s-process elements, and total C+N+O abundance (M. D. Lehnert et al. 1991; G. S. Da Costa et al. 2009; A. F. Marino et al. 2009, 2011b; A. Alves-Brito et al. 2012; M. McKenzie et al. 2022), while photometric studies have revealed the characteristic split RGB and SGB associated with its anomalous populations (A. F. Marino et al. 2009; G. Piotto et al. 2012; J.-W. Lee 2015; A. P. Milone et al. 2017). Intriguingly, the anomalous stars of M22 also display similar light-element patterns observed among canonical populations. In particular, they exhibit C–N, O–Na, and Mg–Al anticorrelations analogous to those that distinguish 1P and 2P stars (A. F. Marino et al. 2011b; J.-W. Lee 2023). This combination of Type II signatures and internal multiple-population patterns has motivated the development of several formation scenarios.

## ABSTRACT 

Globular clusters (GCs) are well known to host stellar populations characterized by light-element variations. A subset of Galactic GCs, beyond such ’canonical’ populations, contains an additional group enriched in iron, s-process elements, and total C+N+O abundance (i.e., the anomalous stars). We combine multi-facility photometry with APOGEE spectroscopy to investigate the spatial distribution, chemical properties, and formation history of the stellar populations in M22, with particular focus on its anomalous component. We trace the canonical and anomalous populations, together with their subpopulations, from the cluster center out to eight half-mass radii. The anomalous population becomes increasingly dominant in the outermost regions, whereas no significant radial gradients are detected among its subpopulations. Our chemical analysis reveals light-element anticorrelations within both the canonical and anomalous components, although the latter are shifted toward higher C, N, and Al abundances. For the first time, we show that the Fe, s-process, and C+N+O enhancements among anomalous stars are not uniform but correlate with their light-element composition: the most chemically extreme anomalous stars are also the most Fe-, Ce-rich, and C+N+O-poor. We identify a distinct red overdensity on the horizontal branch, likely populated by the most He-poor stars, and tentatively associate the extreme horizontal branch with the most chemically enriched anomalous population. These observations are difficult to reconcile with M22 being a merger between two GCs. Instead, they qualitatively favor a self-enrichment scenario regulated by dilution, similar to that recently proposed for _ω_ Centauri, with their close chemical correspondence suggesting that they experienced analogous formation histories.

## ABSTRACT 

Gyrochronology ties stellar rotation periods to ages. It is well studied in the young, open cluster age domain, but there are few constraints on gyrochronology in the old field star regime. In this work we use gyro-kinematic ages to explore the spin down of stars in this formerly inaccessible domain. Using forward modeling techniques which relax strict Rossby scaled assumptions, we find evidence for a departure from a standard spin down models. This departure can be explained with a mass-dependent term either in the global strength of the stellar wind or in the relationship between angular velocity and wind strength. Models with this additional massdependence help explain prior difficulty in fitting open cluster rotation distributions across the full mass range. Additionally, we use rotation models to identify an mass-dependent age domain over which wind driven stellar spin down can be isolated from other physical effects. For lower mass stars, this age domain is most affected by the core-envelope coupling timescale, where as higher mass stars are more subject to inertial effects late in their main sequence lifetimes. Using simple, analytic models of stellar spin down in this domain is unable to determine whether the stellar wind has a mass-dependence or if the stellar wind is strictly Skumanich-like in nature. In future studies of rotational and dynamo evolution we advocate for a forward modeling approach to gyrochronology over purely empirical approaches due to its superior ability to trace physical effects governing stellar spin down.

## 5. CONCLUSION 

In this work, we introduced `flexAE` , a novel and adaptable AE architecture designed to identify unresolved binary systems using multi-band photometry. This framework is, in simple terms, essentially a multidimensional CMD. However, we are able to use information from all available bands simultaneously and explicitly account for observational uncertainties. Furthermore, the AE finds the most efficient way to classify single stars and binary systems in this high-dimensional parameter space, as opposed to following an isochrone. 

It also organizes its latent space in such a way that is optimal for classification by training a classifier component at the same time as the encoder and decoder components. Another main advantage of this approach is that, in principle, we could be sensitive to binary systems with lower mass-ratios (and thus lower flux ratios), though it depends on the quality of the photometry and wavelength coverage. Finally, it is trivial to add additional bands to the analysis as they become available. 

We use `flexAE` to find MS+MS binaries in the outskirts of 47 Tucanae. (a) Presence and persistence of low-density volume-filling gas:
- H II regions in NGC 628: Luminous giant and supergiant H II regions show a decrease in the ionized-gas filling factor (FF) with increasing volume, meaning larger regions are characterized by more widely spaced clumps and a larger fraction of low-density gas occupying the available volume. However, volume alone explains little of the FF scatter (R^2_fit ≃ 0.16–0.21) [evidence_id: 03f11027f87d37771b2883f0].
- Multi-SN bubbles: In bubbles evolved in a clumpy medium, dust (and associated material) can be dispersed into the hot interior and remain there on longer timescales (several Myr) when SN explosions are frequent (more frequent than one per ~30 kyr). The hot interior can thus contain dispersed material and remain a bright IR source for Myr timescales; the hot plasma is maintained at ~2–4×10^6 K for SN rates of one per ~100–5 kyr [evidence_id: 55a5a7dd2fdaf75ac9b7baa4].

(b) Factors controlling amount and observational signatures of low-density gas and differences between papers:
- H II regions (NGC 628): The key control is structural clump spacing within the ionized region: larger physical volume implies more widely spaced clumps and a larger fraction of low-density gas. However, the paper emphasizes that volume alone is insufficient to explain the observed FF scatter, implying additional physical factors (e.g., internal structure, density variations, catalog/method choices) influence FF [evidence_id: 03f11027f87d37771b2883f0; also discussion of methodological effects on measured relations in D.1 indicates which observables are radius-independent and which are not, affecting interpretation].
- Multi-SN bubbles: The dominant controls are the ambient medium structure (clumpiness / density contrast) and the SN cadence. In a clumpy medium, stripped dense lumps and swept-up dust replenish the hot interior, prolonging IR emission; high SN frequency prevents dust exhaustion and sustains hot tenuous gas and IR/X-ray signatures. The IR-to-X-ray luminosity ratio for multi-SN bubbles typically ranges ~1–30 and depends weakly on SN rate but strongly on ambient density contrast (higher destruction of clouds in more homogeneous media reduces IR emission) [evidence_id: 55a5a7dd2fdaf75ac9b7baa4].

Summary synthesis: Both studies identify low-density, volume-filling components in their systems (ionized low-density gas in large H II regions; hot tenuous gas in multi-SN bubbles). The H II-region result attributes larger low-density fraction primarily to geometrical/structural scaling (larger regions with more widely spaced clumps) but finds volume alone is a poor predictor, whereas the multi-SN bubble study attributes persistence and observational visibility of low-density hot gas mainly to dynamical factors (SN frequency) and the ambient medium clumpiness, which determine dust survival and IR vs X-ray emission balance [evidence_id: 03f11027f87d37771b2883f0; 55a5a7dd2fdaf75ac9b7baa4].

## **ABSTRACT** 

Dwarf galaxies located in low density environments that have quiescent stellar populations are extremely rare and the mechanism for quenching their stars is highly uncertain. Here we present two low surface brightness dwarf galaxies with large ( _>_ 1.2 kpc) effective radii that were previously identified in the Dragonfly Ultrawide Survey for which we have obtained spectra using the KCWI instrument on the Keck II telescope. We derive their stellar populations and star formation histories in several radial bins out to 1.25 effective radii. Globally both galaxies are old (∼9 Gyr) and metal-poor ([M/H] ∼ –1) and reveal quenching on a relatively rapid timescale (∼ 1 Gyr). We find flat-to-rising age and metallicity gradients in both galaxies. This is similar to those seen in ultra diffuse galaxies but is in contrast with typical classical dwarf galaxies and predictions from simulations. One galaxy, DFUWS 68, hosts several globular clusters which we find to share similar ages, metallicities and quenching timescales to that of the host galaxy stars. We briefly discuss possible quenching mechanisms and suggest that neither cosmic web stripping nor internal feedback processes alone can explain our results. 

**Key words:** galaxies: dwarf – galaxies: star clusters: general – galaxies: star formation

## **8 CONCLUSIONS** 

In this paper, we have presented deep HST ACS and WFC3 photometry of the entire GC populations of three Local Group dwarfs, comprising 26 GCs in total: the isolated dIrr galaxy, NGC 6822, and the M31 dE satellites, NGC 147 and NGC 185. With this data, we have analysed, for the first time, deep CMDs extending below the HB for GCs in dwarf galaxies beyond the immediate surroundings of the MW. From these CMDs, we quantified the RGB and HB morphologies and used empirical relationships to derive metallicities, line-of-sight extinctions and distances. 

Despite their very different evolutionary histories, we find no evidence for strong differences in the metallicity distributions of the three dwarf galaxies, either in their dispersion or in their mean values. an overall range of −0 _._ 7 ≲[Fe/H] ≲ −2 _._ 5). Their mean metallicity values are likewise very similar, at ∼−1 _._ 6 dex in NGC 6822 and ∼−1 _._ 7 dex in both NGC 147 and NGC 185. We have extensively compared our CMD-based metallicity and reddening measurements with values reported in the literature, most of which are derived using completely independent techniques. Overall, we find very good agreement, and where discrepancies do arise, they can generally be understood.

## **ABSTRACT** 

We present a theoretical framework to derive redshift-dependent metallicity calibrations for galaxies at _𝑧_ =2-7. The ionization parameter ( _𝑈_ ) and gas pressure ( _𝑃_ ) in our approach are not assumed, but are predicted self-consistently. By combining the ASTRID cosmological simulation with stellar population synthesis (SPS) and MAPPINGS V photoionization modeling, we evolve young star clusters under an analytic wind-driven bubble model. This directly couples stellar feedback to the local ISM density, allowing H ii region properties to emerge from the underlying physics rather than being treated as free parameters. The emission-line predictions are validated against observed star-formation rate indicators (deviation <0.05 dex) and the [O iii] luminosity function. We derive calibrations for common optical (e.g. R23, O3N2, N2, O32) and UV (e.g. C3O3, N3O3) diagnostics. We find significant redshift evolution in these relations, driven primarily by changing ionization conditions. A Bayesian analysis quantifies calibration performance under varying signal-to-noise, enabling diagnostic recommendations as a function of redshift and data quality. The R23 calibration performs well at all redshifts with minimal error in our model, while nitrogen- and carbon-based calibrations are highly sensitive to the abundance enrichment process and should be used with caution. These results provide a practical framework for interpreting JWST spectroscopy and tracing chemical evolution from cosmic noon to the epoch of reionization. 

**Key words:** Metallicity – H II regions – High-redshift galaxies

`MAPPINGS V` 5.2.0 photoionization code to compute the emissionline luminosities from the H ii regions surrounding the star clusters. Mappings solves the equations of thermal equilibrium and ionization balance for a nebula with specified physical conditions, yielding the strengths of key optical and UV emission lines. 

In the configuration of the model, we assume a spherical geometry with constant internal pressure throughout the nebula. This choice is physically motivated by the wind-driven bubble model described in Sect. 2.4, where the pressure is dynamically determined by the mechanical feedback from the central star cluster. The pressure input for each H ii region is calculated directly from Eq. 5. The end condition is radiation bounded ( _𝑛_ H II/( _𝑛_ H I + _𝑛_ H II) < 5%), which means low ionizing photons leakage. However, in fact, a significant fraction of ionizing photons can escape the H ii region, which can form Diffuse Ionized Gas (DIG), or even escape to the circumgalactic medium (CGM), contributing to the reionization of the universe. This escaping effect will be discussed in Sect. 5.3. 

The elemental abundances used in the photoionization calculations are drawn directly from the ASTRID simulation for the seven tracked species (C, N, O, Ne, Mg, Si, Fe), supplemented with our estimated sulfur abundance as described in Sect. 2.3.2. Thus, the metallicity of stars and H ii regions is derived from star particles and gas particles, respectively. In our photoionization modeling, dust extinction is neglected to simplify our model. This is physically motivated by observations showing that galaxies at _𝑧>_ 6 are significantly bluer and have a lower infrared excess compared to lower-redshift counterparts (e.g., Capak et al. 2015; Naidu et al. 2022; Barger & Cowie 2023).

## **Abstract** 

Open clusters remain among the most powerful laboratories for calibrating how fundamental stellar properties such as rotation, magnetic activity, surface chemistry, and internal structure evolve over a star’s pre-main-sequence to main-sequence and post-main-sequence lifetime. Because cluster members share a common age, galactic environment, and initial composition, they provide empirical anchors upon which age-dating techniques such as gyrochronology, activity-age relations, and chemical clocks are built. This paper summarizes the Cool Stars 23 splinter session “Open Clusters as Laboratories for Cool Star Evolution”, held on 15 June 2026 in Tokyo, Japan. The session comprised one invited review, ten contributed talks, and ten poster pop-up presentations, organized around three themes: the evolution of rotation, magnetic activity, and chemical abundances (Li-depletion, [C/N], [Y/Mg], and neutron-capture elements). We close with a summary of the open questions identified in the panel discussion and the observational and theoretical work that new surveys (e.g. _Gaia_ DR4, 4MOST, WEAVE) and missions (e.g. PLATO, Roman) will enable over the coming years. Together, these efforts will help assess the current state of the field and shape its future directions.

The chemical homogeneity of most of these structures suggests that they may be remnants of evaporated (or still evaporating) open clusters or objects that formed in star formation hubs where OCs form connected by (or embedded in) bridges of stars. Such hubs can be represented by hierarchical formation structures called LISCA objects (Dalessandro et al. 2021; Della Croce et al. 2023). This seems to be supported by the similarity of the ages of the objects and the OCs embedded in them (see Fig. 5), suggesting that the objects and associated OCs may have been born together. In these cases, the resulting strings may preserve differences in chemical abundances at different locations of the interstellar cloud which could be original or generated by chemical pollution in the neighborhood of massive stars that died via Type II SNe (Großschedl et al. 2026). A possible example of such a formation scenario is provided by the string Theia 216, which exhibits clues of chemical gradients for some elements. 

We saw that what we generically call strings may actually refer to a variety of structures with different origins and evolutions, from evaporating open clusters to dispersing star formation hubs, and original interstellar matter filaments that experienced star formation along their extension to moving groups kinematically triggered by spiral arms or the Galactic bar. More chemical and kinematic data are needed to confirm the findings of this work and provide new information to ensure a better definition of such structures. 

The upcoming _Gaia_ DR4 will provide more data of better quality. Future surveys such as the WHT Enhanced Area Velocity Explorer (WEAVE, Dalton et al. 2012, 2016; Jin et al. 2024) and the 4-metre Multi-Object Spectroscopic Telescope (4MOST, de Jong et al. 2019), equipped with multi-object spectroscopic instruments, will allow us to target such elongated structures and provide precise chemical abundances and radial velocities for a high number of members. A more robust statistics will help us to better constrain the physical conditions of the locations they originated from.

results.question: Compare the methods and main quantitative findings about cluster membership and substellar populations in the two studies: "EWOCS-IX: JWST/NIRCam observations of Westerlund 2 - Identification of candidate substellar members" and "The Comprehensive Investigations of the NGC 7419 Open Cluster and the New Perspective on Mass Populations". Specifically, (a) what membership or contamination-control approaches did each study use, and (b) what are the key quantitative results each reports about low-mass/substellar objects or mass populations (report numerical values stated in the papers)?
results.reference_answer:
a) Membership / contamination-control approaches:
- EWOCS-IX: Characterizes contamination by observing a nearby control field (CF) with identical filter coverage and observing strategy to enable statistical decontamination of the science field; performs PSF photometry with DOLPHOT and validates SED-fitting against synthetic JWST photometry of spectroscopically confirmed young brown dwarfs and simulated field contaminants to ensure robustness against reddened evolved stars (evidence: 4a5be3cb6eead38c3b4245e7; 87034cc1c6f388e66f9825f5).
- NGC 7419 study: Uses the HDBSCAN clustering algorithm within the pyUPMASK framework on five-dimensional Gaia DR3 astrometric space to assign kinematic membership probabilities, thereby separating cluster members from the dense Galactic background and isolating outliers as noise (evidence: 51314b7918ebd1b8131a89f2).

b) Key quantitative results about low-mass/substellar objects or mass populations:
- EWOCS-IX (Westerlund 2): The JWST/NIRCam dataset (10 wide/medium filters spanning 1.15–4.1 μm) reaches a 50% completeness limit at 0.015–0.02 M⊙ (~15–20 M_Jup) for the adopted distance (4.44 kpc), age (1–2 Myr), and A_V = 6.5 mag. Applying their validated SED-fitting methodology they identify 353 substellar candidates, of which 301 are classified as strong candidates and 52 as weak candidates. Comparison with the control field indicates the contamination level of the strong candidate sample is ≲5% down to masses of ~0.01–0.015 M⊙. They also identify 73 substellar candidates exhibiting infrared excess consistent with circumstellar disks; among those with reliable F410M photometry these represent 27.7(+3.4/−3.3)% of that subsample (evidence: 4a5be3cb6eead38c3b4245e7; 87034cc1c6f388e66f9825f5; 9b88ba4ffbfdd86c9401be27).
- NGC 7419 study: The membership pipeline was applied to 5,784 sources within 12′ of the cluster centre to derive kinematic membership probabilities. From orbital integrations (galpy) they report a high total peculiar spatial velocity V_LSR = 102.84 ± 3.00 km s−1 and, regarding mass distribution, they find that NGC 7419's mass distribution is best described by a three-component Gaussian model (i.e., three statistically distinct 'mass populations'), a result they quantify qualitatively and note was reproduced in another cluster (NGC 2168) (evidence: 51314b7918ebd1b8131a89f2; a8d5342f38ed3805a8102144; b4d37a99e7b52cc02d2e5470).

Summary comparison: EWOCS-IX relies on matched control-field observations plus photometric SED-fitting validation to statistically decontaminate and characterize a deep substellar census down to ~0.015 M⊙ with low contamination (~≤5%) among strong candidates, and reports a substantial disk-bearing fraction (~28%) among those with reliable mid-NIR photometry. The NGC 7419 study uses astrometric clustering (HDBSCAN in pyUPMASK) on Gaia DR3 to produce a high-purity membership catalogue for several thousand stars, reports unusual kinematics (V_LSR ≈ 102.8 km s−1) and a multicomponent (three-Gaussian) stellar mass distribution rather than focusing on substellar census (evidence: all cited).

a) The study on Westerlund 2 used spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting with atmospheric models, validation with synthetic photometry, and empirical thresholds to identify candidate substellar members, also applying photometric selection criteria based on color-magnitude diagrams (CMDs) and extinction estimates. The NGC 7419 study employed statistical modeling of stellar mass distributions, fitting Gaussian mixtures to identified mass populations, and comparative analysis with other clusters like NGC 2168 and NGC 6791, focusing on mass distribution characteristics rather than direct member identification.

b) For Westerlund 2, they identified 353 substellar candidates with an estimated contamination level below 5%, detecting objects down to about 0.015-0.02 solar masses, with a total of 308 candidates after selection. In contrast, NGC 7419's study identified multiple statistically significant mass populations via Gaussian mixture models, demonstrating the presence of multiple mass groups, but specific numerical values for individual mass populations are not provided in the excerpts.

## _4.3. Identification of substellar candidates in Westerlund 2_ 

We now apply the validated SED-fitting procedure to the NIRCam photometry of Wd2 in Module B. In addition to selecting the sources with the best-fit _T_ eff ≤ 3000 K, we require them to be located below the theoretical BD boundary in the F150WF200W vs. F150W CMD (black dotted line in Fig. 2), ensuring consistency with substellar luminosities at the distance and age of the cluster. This luminosity cut also removes the brightest substellar binaries with high mass ratios. Assuming a binary fraction similar to that of the ONC (∼12%; De Furio et al. 2022), and considering that only systems near the substellar limit (∼0.050.075 _M_ ⊙) would be excluded by this criterion, we estimate that this effect would cause us to miss less than 10% of the true substellar population. The separation between foreground and cluster sources is clear in the F150W-F200W vs. F150W CMD, allowing us to reliably avoid foreground contamination. We further exclude sources more than 3σ bluer than the _AV_ = 5 mag 1 Myr isochrone in this CMD (black dashed line in Fig. 12). Of the 8324 sources in the Module B catalog, 2599 satisfy these CMDbased selection criteria and are subsequently fitted with the atmospheric model grid. Among them, 590 have best-fit temperatures of _T_ eff ≤ 3000 K in both the full and restricted SED fits. Applying the SED fit empirical χ[2] thresholds derived from the validation sample, yields 308 candidate substellar members.

## **ABSTRACT** 

_Context._ Investigating substellar populations in young massive clusters offers crucial insights into the formation of brown dwarfs (BDs) and the role of environmental conditions in shaping their properties. Westerlund 2 (Wd2), as one of the nearest dense and massive clusters in the Milky Way, represents an ideal laboratory for studying the effffects of high stellar density and ionizing radiation from massive stars on BD formation. _Aims._ This paper presents deep JWST//NIRCam observations of Wd2 in a large number of filters between 1.15 and 4.1 µ _m_ . Our analysis focuses on identifying and characterizing the BD population within the cluster. _Methods._ We carried out PSF photometry on deep JWST/NIRCam/NIRCamNIRCam data obtained in 4 wide and 6 medium-band filters, using DOLPHOT. The resulting catalog was used to identify BD candidates in Wd2 through spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting with atmospheric models. The methodology was validated using synthetic JWST photometry of spectroscopically confirmed young BDs together with simulated populations of typical contaminants, allowing us to define an empirical selection criteria. _Results._ The 50% detection limit of our NIRCam catalog is ∼ ∼0.015-0.02 _M_ ⊙, at the distance, age, and extinction of Wd2, providing the deepest view of a supermassive star cluster to date. The validation demonstrates that the adopted SED-fitting methodology reliably recovers young brown dwarfs while remaining robust against contamination from reddened evolved stars. Applying this procedure to Wd2, we identify 353 substellar candidates. Most candidates (301) lie above the 10 Myr isochrone in the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram consistent with cluster membership, which are defined as strong candidates. Comparison with a control field indicates a contamination level of ≲5% for the strong candidate sample down to masses of ∼0.01–0.0150.01–0.015 _M_ ⊙.. We identify 73 candidates exhibiting infrared excess indicative of circumstellar disks.

The methodology was subsequently applied to the young open cluster NGC 2168, where the stellar mass distribution was also found to be better represented by a multicomponent Gaussian model, with three statistically significant mass populations identified (Ahmed et al. 2026). This result provided an independent example of a multicomponent stellar mass distribution and further demonstrated the applicability of the mass-population framework to young open clusters. The study subsequently received considerable attention and was featured by _Phys.org_[2] . The present analysis demonstrates that NGC 7419 also contains multiple statistically distinct mass populations. The occurrence of similar multicomponent stellar mass distributions in NGC 7419 and NGC 2168, together with the earlier detection of mass populations in the old open cluster NGC 6791, suggests that this phenomenon is not unique to a particular cluster or age. The remarkable similarities between NGC 7419 and NGC 2168 are summarized in Table 11. Both clusters are associated with the Perseus spiral arm, have comparable Galactocentric distances, contain Classical Be stars, and exhibit multiple statistically distinct mass populations despite their different ages. These results motivate a detailed investigation of the physical origin of the observed mass populations and raise the possibility that multicomponent mass distributions may be a broader characteristic of Galactic open clusters.

We also report the discovery of a sequence of unresolved triple and quadruple systems in this cluster, providing spectroscopic confirmation of some of the multiple systems. Within the uncertainties, the fraction of multiple stars in this cluster is comparable to that of the solar neighborhood, with the caveat that the local sample probes deeper down the main sequence. This fraction of unresolved triples and quadruples is also higher than that of the open cluster M 67, which has the same age and chemical composition.

Unresolved triples and quadruples have been previously detected in some young open clusters and associations with ages of _t_ < 100 Myr (e.g., Gonzalez et al., 2014; Tokovinin, 2023; Malofeeva et al., 2023). ## **ABSTRACT** 

_Context._ It is difficult to identify unresolved triple and higher-order systems beyond the solar vicinity. Star clusters yield controlled environments with known physical parameters, providing a way to explore homogeneous stellar samples. 

_Aims._ Combining modern optical and near-IR surveys, our main goal is to explore the region of the color-magnitude diagrams located above the sequence of equal-mass binaries, which is inhabited by unresolved triple and quadruple systems. Specifically, here we aim to discover and characterize the presence of multiple systems in the aged open star cluster Trumpler 19. _Methods._ We selected cluster members using Gaia astrometry and photometry from the VVVX and DECAPS2 surveys. We made optical and near-IR color-magnitude diagrams to select stars located > 0.75 mag above the cluster main sequence, including suitable unresolved triple and quadruple systems. 

- _Results._ We confirm previous results that there is a sizable sequence of unresolved binaries in Trumpler 19. We also report the discovery of a sequence of unresolved multiple systems in this cluster, and confirm some of these multiple systems via radial velocities measured by the ESO KMOS VVVX-GalCen spectroscopic survey. The fraction of multiple stars in this cluster is comparable to that of the solar neighborhood, with the caveat that the local sample probes deeper down the main sequence. The fraction of unresolved triples and quadruples is also three times higher than that of the open cluster M 67, which is of a similar age and chemical composition. 

_Conclusions._ The discovery of unresolved triple systems in Trumpler 19 leads to our main conclusion that these systems were able to survive within the cluster for nearly 4 Gyr. In addition, this cluster contains more multiple systems than M 67, which has a similar total present mass. Further investigations are needed to unveil if this is a primordial feature or the result of dynamical evolution.

(a) The NGC 1052 paper ('Tidal origin of dark-matter free dwarf galaxies in the NGC 1052 group') suggests that dark-matter-deficient dwarfs are produced during a major galaxy merger that creates tidal tails and tidal dwarf galaxies (TDGs). These TDGs are composed of tidal material resulting from the merger, which is naturally free of dark matter. The key spatial constraint predicted is that these DM-free dwarfs should be aligned along tidal tails, remnants of the merger event, and associated with the long-lived tidal features and tails produced in the simulation.

(b) The Little Red Dots paper ('The Ashes of Supermassive Stars: Globular Cluster-like Aluminum Enhancement in Little Red Dots') advocates that a specific nucleosynthetic source—likely supermassive stars—must be responsible for producing the observed strong aluminum (Al) enhancement with magnesium (Mg) depletion. The observational/analysis method involves spectroscopic measurements that reveal chemical abundance patterns within these systems.

(c) The nucleosynthetic requirements for producing strong Al enhancements with Mg depletion in Little Red Dots could potentially be originating from the nuclear processes in supermassive stars, which are different from the formation mechanisms discussed for the DM-deficient dwarfs in the NGC 1052 paper. The NGC 1052 scenario involves tidal interactions during galaxy mergers producing TDGs that lack dark matter but does not explicitly discuss the internal stellar nucleosynthesis or abundance patterns such as Al enrichment. The limitations noted in the NGC 1052 papers concern the broad parameter space and resolution constraints, which prevent precise reproduction of observed features, including detailed chemical abundances. Therefore, while the tidal dwarf galaxy formation could, in principle, host complex stellar populations capable of nucleosynthesis, the specific Al enhancement with Mg depletion described in the Little Red Dots paper requires nucleosynthetic processes (likely in supermassive stars) not addressed explicitly in the tidal formation scenario. Thus, creating systems with the observed chemical peculiarities may involve additional processes beyond tidal formation, and the current tidal models do not seem to explicitly incorporate the necessary nucleosynthesis to produce such chemical signatures.

## **ABSTRACT** 

The discovery of dark matter-free (DM-free) dwarf galaxies in the NGC 1052 neighborhood has had a considerable impact on modern cosmology. The galaxies have been explained through a dwarf–dwarf head-on collision, a rare event. We find that they could alternatively be associated with a head-on 1:1 merger after it was tuned to generate the E4 morphology of NGC 1052. Our simulations show that such mergers produce long-lived tidal features, are associated with the remnant galaxy, and are in the form of large tidal tails, including tidal dwarf galaxies (TDGs). We emphasise that such tidal features are predicted by the hierarchical scenario in which massive galaxies are formed by galaxy mergers. The latter can reproduce both the tidal features in the NGC1052 outskirts and the observed dwarf galaxies. The simulated TDGs have sizes similar to those observed, while they are ten times smaller in the bullet dwarf scenario. However, we cannot reproduce the luminous globular cluster systems due to resolution limitations. Resolving the radial distance between the DM-free dwarfs is necessary to identify the scenario of their formation. We suggest that there should be many other examples of DM-free dwarf galaxies in the neighbourhood of local massive galaxies and galaxy groups. 

**Key words.** Elliptical galaxies – dark matter – merger – dynamics

## **1. Introduction** 

NGC1052-DF2 (Müller et al. 2019). Using numerical simulations, Bournaud & Duc (2006) showed that tidal satellites should be found more frequently around early-type galaxies. The formation of an elliptical galaxy has been modelled by, for example, Wang et al. (2020) to reproduce the properties of Cen A. Both Cen A and NGC 1052 have Seyfert 2 type active nuclei and massive black holes (Wang et al. 2020; Koss et al. 2022), whose formation and growth are likely related to mergers (Hopkins et al. 2006). 

The discovery of dark matter (DM) deficient dwarf galaxies in the NGC 1052 group has attracted considerable attention and generated many debates over the past 8 years (van Dokkum et al. 2018, 2019). For example, Monelli & Trujillo (2019) argued that the mass based on dynamics of surrounding globular clusters (GCs) of NGC1052-DF2 could have been underestimated due to a distance overestimate. However, a more accurate distance based on the tip of the red giant branch (TRGB) stars has been obtained (Shen et al. 2021), confirming the distance of two DMdeficient dwarfs, DF2 and DF4, at ∼ 20 Mpc (see also Tang et al. 2026). 

In this paper we investigate whether the chain of DMdeficient dwarfs could be associated with a tidal tail, which would have been formed during a merger similar to that described by Wang et al. (2020). The goal is not to fully reproduce the observations of the NGC 1052 field but to verify whether this hypothesis may be compelling in comparison with the bullet dwarf model described by Lee et al. (2024) and by Keim et al. (2025). In Sect. 2 we describe the mechanism and associated parameters necessary to form an elliptical galaxy such as Cen A and NGC 1052. Section 3 shows how such a model may generate tidal tails and associated tidal dwarfs, and we also compare how realistically it may reproduce the observations. In Sect. 4 we compare and discuss the strengths and weaknesses of the two competitive models, the result of which is summarised in Section 5.

## **5. Conclusions** 

In this work, we have verified that a major merger experienced by NGC 1052 produces tidal tails and TDGs that match the intrinsic properties of DM-deficient dwarfs discovered by van Dokkum et al. (2018, 2019) as well as their alignment along a trail. Our finding results from simple adaptations of the N- body hydrodynamical simulations made by Wang et al. (2020) to reproduce the properties of Cen A, and we addressed the supposed failures of the TDG scenario. The only limitation of our - modelling comes from its very large parameter space and insuffi ciently precise constraints on NGC 1052 and associated dwarfs, which prevented us from experimenting with a more accurate reproduction of the observations. 

According to the hierarchical scenario, the present-day E4 morphology of NGC 1052 takes its origin from its last major merger, which requires radial orbits, moderate gas fraction, a mass ratio close to 1:1, and specific orientations of the progenitor galaxies (Wang et al. 2020). The latter conditions are necessary to remove most of the angular momentum in the remnant, which is currently accompanied by large tidal tails and TDGs and match better the observations when compared to the bulletdwarf scenario. 

The bullet-dwarf scenario suffers from two major difficulties: first, reproducing the dwarf progenitors and, second, providing far too compact DM-deficient dwarfs. The scenario also neglects the fact that NGC 1052 is an active nucleus E4 galaxy showing tides, and it has likely experienced a major merger that can produce TDGs resembling the observed DM-deficient dwarfs. The likely occurrence of massive galaxy mergers near NGC 1052 has to be compared to the very rare dwarf–dwarf collision events in the field, for which only ten have been found in a (100Mpc)[3] volume from _z_ =3 to _z_ =0 (Lee et al. 2024). Future observations of dwarf radial distances will probe which of the two scenarios is the most likely. The dwarf GC over-luminosity appears to support the bullet-dwarf scenario, though there might be subtle selection effects associated with this property.

results.question: Compare the evidence and proposed observational follow-ups in (1) "The youngest white dwarf companion to a millisecond pulsar: Insights from NGC 362D" and (2) "Planetary Nebula Central Stars as Tracers of Planetary Nebula–Star Cluster Associations in the Galaxy" regarding the role of spectroscopy for constraining companion/central-star properties. Specifically: which concrete spectral diagnostics does paper (1) propose to search for to test the residual circumstellar-material scenario for COM-NGC362D, and what broader spectroscopic needs and limitations does paper (2) identify for improving central-star (CS) parameter estimates? Provide an explicit synthesis that draws on both papers' recommendations.
results.reference_answer:
Paper (1) "The youngest white dwarf companion to a millisecond pulsar: Insights from NGC 362D" proposes concrete spectroscopic diagnostics: detection of narrow metal lines (explicitly motivated by detections in PSR J1816+4510) such as He I, Ca II, Si II, and Mg II, and measurement of the companion radial-velocity curve to constrain the binary mass ratio (evidence: e16574046febb2cf0a447e2d; d2c9f58109af70350b291b7c). Paper (1) links these metal-line detections to the presence of a lower-pressure environment associated with an expelled cloud of circumstellar material and suggests such lines would support the residual-material interpretative scenario (evidence: d2c9f58109af70350b291b7c).

Paper (2) "Planetary Nebula Central Stars as Tracers of Planetary Nebula–Star Cluster Associations in the Galaxy" identifies broader spectroscopic needs and limitations: it stresses the lack of adequate data for precise CS effective-temperature estimates as a major limitation for assessing candidate CS–cluster associations, and recommends deep spectroscopic nebular data and photoionization modelling to derive more precise CS physical properties (evidence: 043cf2bd326941e493456f18). It also notes that uncertainties in CS temperatures and luminosities (and assumptions made when temperatures are unavailable) limit evolutionary consistency checks (evidence: 20b09817ecfa63e067864be0).

Synthesis: Both papers converge on spectroscopy as a critical next step but at different, complementary levels. The MSP-WD study (paper 1) calls for high-resolution optical spectroscopy of the companion to (a) measure radial velocities (dynamical masses) and (b) detect narrow metal absorption lines (He I, Ca II, Si II, Mg II) that would be direct diagnostics of low-pressure expelled circumstellar material. The PN–cluster study (paper 2) emphasizes the need for deep nebular and stellar spectroscopy plus photoionization modelling to improve CS effective-temperature and luminosity estimates, which are necessary to test evolutionary consistency with cluster ages and the initial–final mass relation. Together, these recommendations imply a coordinated observational approach: for compact binary companions like COM-NGC362D, targeted high-resolution stellar spectroscopy to detect metal lines and radial-velocity variations; for CSs in cluster searches, deep nebular spectra and modelling to infer CS Teff and L. Implementing both types of spectroscopic programs would provide the direct compositional/dynamical diagnostics (paper 1) and the improved physical parameter estimates (paper 2) that are each required to robustly interpret post–mass-transfer objects and to confirm associations with clusters (evidence: e16574046febb2cf0a447e2d; d2c9f58109af70350b291b7c; 043cf2bd326941e493456f18; 20b09817ecfa63e067864be0).
results.answer: Paper (1) suggests that future spectroscopic observations of COM-NGC362D could measure the radial-velocity curve to directly determine the binary mass ratio. Additionally, the detection of narrow metal lines similar to those observed in other systems would support the residual circumstellar material scenario, with lines such as He i, Ca ii, Si ii, and Mg ii being potential diagnostics. Paper (2), while focused on planetary nebula central stars, emphasizes that spectroscopy is essential for deriving fundamental parameters like temperature, gravity, and composition of the central stars. It notes that current limitations include difficulty in obtaining high signal-to-noise ratio spectra for faint or crowded stars, and that accurate line profiles are critical for precise parameter estimates. Broader needs include high-resolution, high-quality spectra to disentangle stellar and nebular contributions, which would improve estimates of stellar parameters and evolutionary status.

## **4. Discussion and conclusions** 

In this letter we report on the identification and characterisation of the optical counterpart to the binary MSP NGC362D using deep, multi-band, and multi-epoch HST observations. Interestingly, COM-NGC362D turns out to be the youngest WD companion to a MSP known to date. Moreover, its photometric properties and its wavelength-dependent variations strongly suggest the presence of residual circumstellar material likely expelled during the mass-transfer phase. Regardless of the exact origin of the material, which remains an open question, this system provides a test case to directly probe the immediate aftermath of the MSP recycling process and to constrain the early evolutionary stages of proto-WD companions and their radio and optical properties. 

In this respect, we note that some of the properties inferred for COM-NGC362D resemble those observed in the enigmatic Galactic-field system PSR J1816+4510 (Kaplan et al. 2012, 2013; Polzin et al. 2020; Shang et al. 2024). This system was initially classified as a RB (Kaplan et al. 2012; Stovall et al. 2014) because of the presence of radio eclipses lasting for 7%– 10% of the orbital period. However, optical spectroscopic studies (Kaplan et al. 2013) revealed a companion with a minimum mass of 0.19 M⊙, Teff = 16000 K and low surface gravity, which are consistent with expectations for a proto-WD. Polzin et al. (2020) reported a transition in the eclipsing mechanism of PSR J1816+4510, from direct flux removal to a simple smearing of the radio signal, which was interpreted as evidence of the presence of an extended tail of material. Moreover, Kaplan et al. (2013) detected narrow He i, Ca ii, Si ii, and Mg ii lines, which could originate in a lower pressure environment possibly associated with this cloud of expelled material. Therefore, it is very tempting to conclude that PSR J1816+4510 and COM-NGC362D share very similar properties and, very likely, a similar evolutionary stage.

## **4 DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS** 

**Comparison with previous pattern speed constraints.** Most recent estimates of the pattern speed are in the range Ωb = 30 − 45 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] (Portail et al. 2017; Sanders et al. 2019; Bovy et al. 2019; Binney 2020; Chiba & Schönrich 2021; Clarke & Gerhard 2022; Li et al. 2022; Leung et al. 2023; Zhang et al. 2024; Dillamore et al. 2025). Our upper bound of ≈ 26 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] inferred from _𝜔_ Cen’s migration is therefore much slower than the general consensus. However, some works have found lower values; Horta et al. (2025) estimate Ωb = 24 ± 3 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] , in good agreement with our result. Hence there remains considerable uncertainty about the pattern speed. However, if values below 26 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] can be definitively ruled out by future studies, this would help to falsify the bar-induced migration scenario.

However, it has become clear in recent years that the Galactic bar causes significant perturbations to orbits in the inner stellar halo (Dillamore et al. 2023, 2024b, 2025; Dillamore & Sanders 2025; Tomlinson et al. 2026; De Leo et al. 2026; Gherghinescu et al. 2026). The bar’s pattern speed Ωb (rotation rate) is likely to be decelerating (Chiba et al. 2021; Zhang et al. 2025), a process which can cause migration of globular clusters via resonances (Dillamore et al. 2024b). These include the retrograde 1:1 resonance, where the orbital frequencies of a particle satisfy Ω _𝜙_ − Ωb + Ω _𝑟_ = 0. Tomlinson et al. (2026) showed that this resonance can cause significant scattering of orbits along its length in ( _𝐿 𝑧, 𝐸_ ) space (on lines of gradient d _𝐸_ /d _𝐿 𝑧_ = Ωb; see Dillamore & Sanders 2025). This process could be responsible for deflecting _𝜔_ Cen onto lower energy, more retrograde orbits (Laporte & Orkney 2026). In this _Letter_ we investigate this scenario by running simulations in a realistic Milky Way potential with a decelerating bar. We determine the range of pattern speeds compatible with the migration of _𝜔_ Cen from the GSE debris, and thus assess how plausible this scenario is. We also analyse the chemical composition of retrograde substructure between the GSE debris and _𝜔_ Cen, extending the analysis of Laporte & Orkney (2026). 

The rest of this _Letter_ is arranged as follows. In Section 2 we describe the data used, and analyse the chemistry of retrograde substructure. Section 3 discusses our simulations and the constraint on Ωb. Finally we discuss and summarise our conclusions in Section 4.

results.question: Compare the conceptual picture and observational priorities for Galactic Center regulation described in the conference overview paper "IAU Symposium 405: Traversing the Galactic Center in Space and Time" with the simulation results from "A new clump-based star formation model for galaxy simulations: implications for high-redshift compact star clusters". Specifically: (a) According to IAU Symposium 405, what processes are proposed to regulate gas inflow and star formation near Sgr A* and the Central Molecular Zone? (b) Which key simulation findings from the CSF paper (include compactness dependence, clump properties, global SFE, bound-cluster formation, and differences versus KS runs) support or contradict the symposium's ecosystem view, and how do they suggest compactness and star-formation prescription influence regulation across scales?
results.reference_answer: (a) The IAU Symposium 405 overview emphasizes that the Galactic Center is an interconnected ecosystem in which black-hole accretion, star formation, stellar feedback, gas dynamics and magnetic fields continuously influence one another; inflowing gas from the bar is largely prevented from reaching Sgr A* because it is converted into stars, dispersed by stellar winds and supernovae, or expelled through outflows from the hot accretion flow, so feedback operating across many spatial scales regulates the nucleus (evidence_id: 8f89309050d61336c355c0fb). (b) The CSF simulations provide concrete, supporting mechanisms showing how compactness and the star-formation prescription modulate that regulation: compact discs form more massive and denser gas clumps (maximum clump mass rises from ~1e5 to 1e7 Msun and surface densities up to >1e4 Msun pc^-2 as compactness increases) and produce higher, burstier global SFE (in 1e10 Msun haloes global SFE at t=3 t_dyn rises from 5e-3 at low compactness to 2e-1 at highest compactness, with peak SFRs ~1 Msun/yr for compact runs), while the most compact systems experience strong feedback that can evacuate central gas (evidence_ids: 0c3dbf13da9dd4027969933c, 160dd9270d4a618cf6df643a). Bound, self-gravitating star clusters form only in sufficiently compact discs (no bound clusters for compactness <=2 in 1e10 Msun haloes; bound-cluster mass fraction reaches ~40% at compactness >=8; threshold depends on halo mass), showing that compactness controls whether inflowing gas is locked into stars vs. dispersed (evidence_id: 9ee13cd7e925ed789689fa3d). The CSF versus KS comparison shows the choice of star-formation model is itself decisive: KS runs keep gas discs intact, have less bursty histories, peak SFRs an order of magnitude lower than CSF at high compactness, and saturate SFE ~5e-2 rather than rising with compactness, implying that small-scale star-formation physics (clump-based vs. KS) alters the efficiency of feedback and thus the multiscale regulatory coupling (evidence_id: 9ee13cd7e925ed789689fa3d). Overall, the CSF results support the symposium's ecosystem picture by demonstrating that disc compactness and local star-formation physics can set clump properties, star-formation efficiency and feedback strength, thereby regulating gas supply to nuclei across scales; they further quantify thresholds (compactness and halo-mass dependence) and show that different subgrid prescriptions change whether gas is retained or expelled, offering a physical route for the processes the symposium highlights (evidence_ids: 8f89309050d61336c355c0fb; 0c3dbf13da9dd4027969933c; 160dd9270d4a618cf6df643a; 9ee13cd7e925ed789689fa3d).
results.answer:
(a) The IAU Symposium 405 emphasizes that the Galactic Center functions as an interconnected ecosystem where gas inflow, star formation, stellar feedback, magnetic fields, and black-hole accretion regulate each other across multiple scales, balancing inflow with feedback-driven outflows and self-regulation of activity.

(b) The CSF simulation results support this ecosystem view by showing that the physical processes, such as star formation efficiency and feedback, depend on the galaxy's compactness, influencing structures like clumps and global star formation rates. The simulations demonstrate that more compact systems tend to have higher star formation efficiency and bound cluster formation, aligning with the idea that feedback and regulation are scale-dependent. Differences between CSF and KS runs highlight the importance of star formation prescriptions, impacting the morphology and star formation activity, thereby reinforcing that regulation mechanisms are sensitive to the physical model and galaxy properties.

## **From the Central Molecular Zone to the event horizon** 

One of the central questions discussed at the symposium concerned the striking contrast between the vast molecular gas reservoir of the CMZ and the extremely low luminosity of Sgr A* (talks by Steven Longmore and Mark Morris). Although the Galactic bar efficiently channels gas towards the inner Galaxy, only a tiny fraction ultimately reaches the black hole. Instead, much of the inflowing material is converted into stars, dispersed by stellar winds and supernova explosions, or expelled through outflows from the hot accretion flow surrounding Sgr A* [2]. The Galactic Center therefore appears to regulate itself through feedback operating across many spatial scales (Zixuan Feng). This perspective also reshapes our understanding of star formation. The CMZ provides a nearby laboratory for studying star formation under conditions resembling those in high-redshift starburst galaxies, with unusually high gas densities, turbulence and magnetic fields. Yet fundamental questions remain unresolved. Young massive stars are observed within the central parsec (Zo¨e Haggard) despite the intense tidal field of Sgr A* and the extreme physical conditions of the surrounding circumnuclear medium [the “paradox of youth”; 3]. ## 8. SUMMARY AND FUTURE WORK 

In this work, we develop a generative model to infer _T_ eff , log _g_ , [Fe _/_ H], [ _α/_ M] from SDSS-V BOSS spectra in DR20. The aim was to develop a model that covered a wide range of the HR diagram, improved on other pipelines used in SDSS-V, and was well-suited for the lower-resolution BOSS dataset. To accomplish this, we developed BOSS-CLAM. BOSS-CLAM forward models spectra by mapper stellar labels to NMF basis vector weights, which are combined with NMF basis vectors to represent BOSS spectra. This mapping and these basis vectors are optimized using a training set consisting of labels from ASPCAP, `MINESweeper` , wide binaries, and a hot star validation sample. Currently, the only pipeline that fits the above criteria is BOSSNet (L. Sizemore et al. 2024). BOSSNet is a data-driven discriminative model that utilizes a neural network to predict _T_ eff , log _g_ , and [Fe _/_ H] from BOSS spectra. For training, it drew labels from a variety of sources in order to cover a significant range of the HR diagram. On average, BOSSNet achieves these goals with high precision. However, there are some issues with these results. Primarily, there are significant systematic errors across the HR diagram. The top row of Figure 1 shows the difference between the stellar pa- 

rameters used for training in this work (True; Section 2) and the BOSSNet parameters. Significant biases are observed, especially for the subgiants and at the most metal-poor end. Additionally, as the model is discriminative, it tends to bias poorly-fitted parameters to the mean of the training distribution. Because of these issues, the goal of this paper is to develop a model that reduces systematic errors and avoids some of the pitfalls of discriminative models. 

In this work we focus on generative, forward-modeling approaches where stellar spectra are estimated from labels. Particularly when training a model with higherprecision labels relative to the spectra themselves, as is the case here, this has significant advantages. As discussed in Y.-S. Ting (2025), when the input features (in this case, lower resolution spectra) have much higher noise than the outputs (stellar labels from higher resolution spectra), this inevitably leads to attenuation bias in discriminative models. In a generative model, as the noisier spectrum is the dependent variable, only the variance of the model estimate is affected, not the bias. Additionally, during inference the uncertainty in the spectra is explicitly incorporated into the likelihood.

## ABSTRACT 

Large spectroscopic surveys require robust pipelines capable of inferring stellar parameters over a wide range of the Hertzsprung-Russell (HR) diagram from data of varying quality. SDSS-V is one such survey, where the data from the lower-resolution, optical BOSS spectrograph will provide a large dataset covering a wide range of Galactic stellar populations. To better analyze these data, we present BOSS-CLAM, a generative, forward modeling pipeline for inferring effective temperature ( _T_ eff ), surface gravity (log _g_ ), metallicity ([Fe _/_ H]), and _α−_ abundance ([ _α/_ M]) from continuum-normalized BOSS spectra.
